analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in full, restoring the law as it stood before.
analysis.headline: The full-repeal bill, backed by 68 Republican cosponsors, was referred to eight House committees and never received a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and the companion 2010 reconciliation law, and restore every provision of law those acts changed, as if they had never passed. That would end the ACA's coverage expansions, its subsidies, its protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and its taxes on high-income households and health-related industries. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be high-income households, who would again escape the ACA's 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax and 3.8% tax on investment income, and industries facing ACA-era taxes and rules, including medical device makers and large employers who would no longer owe penalties for not offering coverage. Insurers would be freed from ACA rules such as the medical loss ratio and rate review, though they would also lose the subsidized customer base the law created.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective as of each law's original enactment [S3].
It restores or revives every provision of law that those acts amended or repealed, putting federal law back exactly where it stood before the ACA [S2] [S3].

Repealing those statutes would remove the ACA's taxes on high earners' wages and investment income, a direct tax cut for the wealthiest households (how the mechanism works: the ACA added a 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax and a 3.8% net investment income tax on upper incomes) [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on people who got coverage through the ACA: those newly eligible for Medicaid, people receiving premium subsidies, adults under 26 on a parent's plan, and people with pre-existing conditions who could previously be denied coverage or charged more. The ACA taxes repealed by the bill would shift that revenue loss onto the broader taxpayer base or add to deficits.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA enrollees and people with pre-existing conditions

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the ACA's coverage expansions and insurance protections in their entirety, with no replacement, which by the law's design would leave people with pre-existing conditions, subsidized enrollees, and new Medicaid beneficiaries without the coverage they gained [S2] [S3].
Because the repeal is retroactive to the laws' original enactment and restores prior law, it offers no transition: provisions people and states had reorganized around would simply vanish [S3].

A good-faith objection its supporters would raise — that the ACA involved mandates, taxes, and federal regulation of a large share of the economy — is a real cost of the law; this bill's answer is to remove all of it at once with nothing in its place, which is the trade an honest supporter must acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated and easy to name: tax relief for the top brackets and removal of taxes and mandates for specific industries. The losses are broad and harder to see from one household to the next — coverage, subsidies, and protections that millions of individuals rely on, all erased at once. Weighed honestly, the bill is a large transfer of security away from ordinary households in favor of tax cuts for concentrated wealth, with no replacement framework.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced the first day of the new Congress, sent to eight different House committees and five subcommittees, and never came back out for a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Steve King of Iowa introduced the ObamaCare Repeal Act on January 6, 2015, with 18 original cosponsors listed in the bill text [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations [S5].

Over the following months it was further referred to subcommittees on Health, Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, Higher Education and Workforce Training, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
After those referrals, no further action was ever recorded; the bill died in committee without a vote in the House or Senate [S5].
In total, 68 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans, and no Democrat did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The households and industries that would have paid the ACA's taxes and followed its mandates are better off because the bill never advanced. The millions of people covered through the ACA were better off as well, since their coverage and protections were never put to a vote. The cosponsoring members also got a stated position on record without ever having to cast a roll-call vote on full repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and ACA enrollees alike

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on the first day of the 114th Congress and recruited 18 original cosponsors from the bill text.

for.name: 68 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican and no Democrat signed on.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker's office, which controls floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to eight committees and never scheduled it for a floor vote, despite their party holding the House majority; no hearing or committee vote was ever scheduled either.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Stood ready to veto ACA repeal legislation and actually vetoed a full-repeal measure passed by Congress later in this same Congress, making passage of any full repeal without overriding him impossible.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.note: Repeal frees insurers from ACA rules (medical loss ratio requirements, rate review, guaranteed-issue mandates) but strips away the subsidized marketplace customers the law delivered them. Their interest in shedding consumer protections runs against the people those protections serve. [S3]
Repeal eliminates the ACA's 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax and 3.8% net investment income tax on upper incomes — a direct tax cut concentrated at the top, with the revenue loss borne broadly. [S3]
Repeal removes the ACA's 2.3% excise tax on medical devices, an industry-specific tax cut whose cost was a funding source for the ACA's coverage expansions. [S3]

Repeal ends the employer mandate and its penalties for not offering affordable coverage, removing a cost for large chains and employers; the burden shifts back onto workers who would have relied on subsidies. [S3]
Repeal removes ACA brand-drug fees and would end the coverage growth that brought drugmakers new paying customers; the industry publicly opposed full repeal for that reason.
